title: Fluctuation--Response Relation in Finite-Size Noisy Coupled Phase Oscillators
abstract: Fluctuation--response relations (FRRs) provide a fundamental relation between spontaneous fluctuations and the linear response to external perturbations, yet their validity in non-equilibrium systems remains an open problem. In a general class of noisy, finite-size, mean-field models of coupled phase oscillators, we reveal two types of FRRs in the incoherent phase below the synchronization transition. The first, corresponding to the infinite-size limit (I-FRR), involves the convolution between the external force and the correlation function in the time domain. The second, the finite-size counterpart (F-FRR), is governed by finite-size fluctuations and carries a correction factor: a spectrum function whose roots correspond to eigenvalues, or Landau poles, of the linear operator. The finite-size fluctuations are suppressed in the weak-coupling or strong-noise limits, and F-FRR reduces to I-FRR. Our analytical findings are verified by extensive numerical simulations.
summary: This work derives and verifies two forms of the Fluctuation-Response Relation for noisy, finite-size coupled phase oscillators. It establishes that the finite-size counterpart (F-FRR) includes a correction factor absent in the infinite-size limit (I-FRR). This is crucial for accurately modeling real, finite physical systems operating far from equilibrium.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental, open problem of establishing the validity of Fluctuation–Response Relations (FRRs) in non-equilibrium, finite-size systems.
main_result: Two distinct FRRs—an Infinite-size (I-FRR) and a Finite-size (F-FRR)—are derived for coupled phase oscillators, with the F-FRR incorporating a crucial finite-size correction factor.
method: The analysis involves linearizing the Dean-Kawasaki equation, solving the resulting equations using Fourier and Laplace transforms, and deriving the relations analytically.
model_or_system: The system is a general class of $N$ globally-coupled phase oscillators, modeled by a noisy mean-field equation resembling the Kuramoto model. The analysis focuses on the dynamics below the synchronization transition.
key_observables: Order parameters ($Z_n(t)$), response function ($R_n(t)$), and various correlation functions ($C_{in,n}(t), C_n(t)$).
important_parameters: Noise strength ($D$), coupling strength ($K$), and system size ($N$). Key regimes include the weak-coupling/strong-noise limits and the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on linearizing the dynamics and making assumptions about scale separation to distinguish response from finite-$N$ fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crossover of correlation functions between transient and stationary regimes, and compare measured response spectra against theoretical I-FRR and F-FRR predictions.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by deriving the I-FRR and F-FRR in the Laplace domain, confirming the F-FRR's necessity via numerical simulations, and finally deriving the time-domain form using Kramers-Kronig relations.
why_interesting: The rigorous derivation of the F-FRR provides a powerful, quantitative tool for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems, extending fundamental fluctuation theorems beyond the infinite-size limit.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic crossover in the D (noise) - τ (time) plane within the nonsynchronized phase. As τ progresses, the tran- sient correlation function Cn(t, τ) (blue), for mode n, crosses over to the time-averaged, stationary correlation function Cn(t) (red); see the main text for their definitions. Additional correlations are generated by finite-size effects while relaxing to the finite-N stationary state, whereas Cn(t) approaches Cini n (t) := Cn(t, τ = 0) as D increases. Cn(t) satisfies the finite-size fluctuation-response relation (F-FRR), while the infinite-size FRR (I-FRR) is satisfied only by Cini n (t).

FIG. 5. Validity of the F-FRR across the (D, K) plane via the normalized time-domain residual ∆. Color encodes, on a log scale, (a) ∆noF and (b) ∆F: ∆≤0.1 (teal) indicat- ing good agreement and ∆≥0.2 (magenta) indicating poor agreement. The threshold is chosen to lie within the sta- tistical fluctuations of the simulations arising from the finite number of realizations [65]. The observation time Tobs = 5 is chosen so that the correlation has decayed to zero. The black region marks the synchronized phase with K > Kc(D) and lies outside the domain of the theory.
